articles.title: People with low implicit self-worth are quicker to notice subtle facial cues of anger and disgust
articles.summary: People with hidden doubts about their self-worth are quicker to spot subtle facial expressions of anger and disgust. New research shows that unconscious self-esteem strongly influences how we perceive social cues and navigate relationships.

articles.title: Scientists trace the nerve pathway that links digestion to memory
articles.summary: A new small study in rats reveals that the digestive tract communicates with the brain during meals to help remember where food was found, a process that can be disrupted by an early-life junk food diet.

articles.title: Why do people protest? Six decades of research points to social connections over personal grievances
articles.summary: A comprehensive review of 60 years of research reveals that people who participate in protests are driven more by social connections and political interest than by personal grievances, anger, or mistrust of the government.

articles.title: Autism is linked to a nearly 14-year shorter life expectancy among Medicaid beneficiaries
articles.summary: A new study indicates that autistic individuals on Medicaid have a life expectancy nearly 14 years shorter than the general U.S. population. This stark gap is largely driven by preventable causes like infections, malnutrition, and fatal accidents.

articles.title: Psilocybin and standard antidepressants both shift the brain away from negative biases
articles.summary: A new study reveals that psilocybin and standard antidepressants both reduce the brain's tendency to misinterpret facial expressions as negative. The research suggests these two distinct treatments share a common cognitive effect in the fight against depression.

articles.title: High testosterone is linked to “loss chasing” behavior after setbacks
articles.summary: Contrary to popular stereotypes, higher testosterone isn't consistently tied to taking more risks. Instead, new research suggests the hormone is associated with how individuals physically process their "gut feelings" after experiencing a win or loss.

articles.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
articles.summary: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging.

articles.summary: As internet access spreads across the globe, formal religious affiliation tends to fall. A new study of 81 countries links three decades of digital expansion to a steady decline in traditional religious identity.

articles.title: These blood thinners may have an unexpected benefit for Alzheimer’s patients
articles.summary: Newer blood thinners may do more than prevent strokes in people with Alzheimer’s disease and atrial fibrillation. Researchers found that patients taking NOACs experienced a slower decline in cognitive function than those using warfarin or no blood thinners. The effect was modest each year but could add up over time.

articles.title: Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.

articles.title: Esketamine-induced dissociation is tied to better outcomes in treatment-resistant depression
articles.summary: Patients with treatment-resistant depression who experienced feelings of unreality during subcutaneous esketamine therapy were more likely to see their depression symptoms improve, suggesting dissociation may be tied to the drug's effectiveness rather than just a side effect.

articles.title: Scientists find that “perfect” systems may be surprisingly fragile
articles.summary: Complex systems may work better when their parts are not perfectly alike. Northwestern physicists found that carefully balanced variation, or “disorder,” can make networks such as power grids, ecosystems, neurons, and materials more stable. Even random differences sometimes improved stability compared with completely uniform systems. The discovery could help researchers design more resilient technologies and explain why natural systems are so rarely perfectly uniform.

articles.title: Memories of childhood scents associated with joy are encoded by neurons generated shortly after birth
articles.summary: A new study reveals that powerful, happy childhood scent memories are encoded by neurons generated just after birth. As we age, the brain reorganizes how it stores these smells, shifting from reward centers to deeper emotional networks.

articles.summary: How does using screens to calm an upset child relate to their developing mind? New research suggests the answer depends on the child, showing that media habits and cognitive skills often forecast each other in a continuous loop.
